Case study A · full attribution release

Why Measurement Systems Disagree

A measurement definition changes which conversions receive credit—even when the underlying event data stays fixed.

16,468,027 impressions · 6,142,256 users · 5,947,563 click indicators · 675 campaigns · 438,730 canonical conversions. Observed CTR: 36.12%.

Why first-click, last-click and linear agree at campaign level

The actual data contains 0 multi-campaign conversion paths and 139,762 paths with multiple clicked impressions. First and last touch can choose different events, but all credit stays in the same campaign. Their campaign counts and ranks therefore coincide at a fixed window. We retain this null result.

Last clicked-impression lag: median 0.86 days; p75 7.15; p90 18.06; p95 23.61. Moving 1→7 days adds 98,408 conversions; 7→14 adds 48,833; 14→30 adds 63,464.

Explore campaign measurement definitions

Top 15 matching campaigns by credit. CVR here = credited conversions / impressions, not a unique-user probability. CPA uses transformed cost units, never advertiser dollars. Publisher output ignores the proxy window.

Event identity, timestamp semantics and attribution rules

Source timestamps are relative seconds, beginning at zero. Calendar date, timezone and independent click time are unavailable. We use clicked-impression time as an explicit proxy. Each source shard + row ordinal is an event ID; replaying that ID is deduplicated while repeated users and valid repeated events are preserved. 2,910 raw conversion IDs recur across different user/time pairs, so canonical identity is (conversion ID, user ID, conversion timestamp).

We reconstruct only source-linked canonical conversion paths. A user-only join across arbitrary campaigns would invent advertiser relationships absent from the release. Eligible clicked impressions satisfy 0 ≤ conversion time − impression time ≤ window × 86,400. Earliest/latest time selects first/last, with click position and stable event ID breaking ties; linear credit is 1 / eligible touches.

The observed click-through conversion share is 100%: every labeled canonical conversion has a linked clicked impression. This describes this release, not the advertiser’s full conversion funnel. Attribution is anchored to selected impression day; source labels can occur after the impression collection period.

What changes with treatment assignment?

Keep all assigned participants in their original arm. Effective ad exposure is a different variable.

Binary outcomes: Newcombe score intervals for the absolute difference; pooled two-proportion z-test. Intervals are marginal under independent-record assumptions; experiment IDs are unavailable for clustering. Sampling and model uncertainty are not captured by these intervals.

Recommendation: report the effect size with uncertainty, not just statistical significance. The release contrast is +115.2 conversions per 100k assigned participants. Validate transport to a new advertiser with a prospective randomized holdout and observed costs before discussing incremental ROAS.

The allocation check against the publisher’s rounded 85% reference gives p = 0.9994. This is not a confirmatory sample-ratio-mismatch test: original randomization probabilities and experiment IDs are missing. Low observed SMDs do not undo release sampling.

P(exposure | treatment) = 3.6037%; P(exposure | control) = 0.0000%. Exposed/unexposed outcomes are supplied only as descriptive diagnostics. No causal exposed-only comparison or IV/LATE estimate is made: exclusion, monotonicity and release-sampling assumptions cannot be verified.

Heterogeneous effects · held-out evaluation

Can targeting concentrate incremental response?

A practical T-learner estimates conversion probability separately in each assignment arm, then ranks by the predicted difference.

Model subset: 2,797,402 real records (~20% feature-group hash sample). Train 1,678,633 · validation 559,705 · test 559,064. Exact feature vectors never cross splits. Assignment, exposure and outcomes never determine the split or enter model features.

Open full-size chart ↗

Test AUUC = 0.00108676; Qini coefficient = 0.00040946 incremental conversions per evaluated participant. Multiply by 100,000 for chart-scale areas: 108.68 and 40.95. Treat-all endpoint = 135.46 conversions / 100k test participants.

Open full-size chart ↗
Recommendation: use the top-response group as a candidate for a new randomized targeting test. The highest predicted decile has observed lift 872.8 / 100k (95% CI 560.1–1,145.4). The lowest predicted decile is also positive: ranking is imperfect and the deciles are not monotonic. These anonymous groups are not demographic audiences or a deployment-ready budget policy.

Model selection and metric definitions

Two histogram gradient-boosted classifiers, 15 leaves, at least 200 records per leaf; 60 and 120 iterations compared on validation Qini. Selected 60 iterations; test was evaluated after selection. No test-based model tuning. f0–f11 have no documented demographic interpretation.

For ranked top fraction q, G(q) = Σ[Y·T/p − Y·(1−T)/(1−p)] / N, with p the observed treatment fraction in that evaluation split. Random targeting is q·G(1), not simulated users. AUUC integrates G; Qini integrates G − random. Equal-score blocks are averaged for curves. Decile boundary ties use stable source IDs, so tied records can span neighboring deciles.

Decile intervals are marginal Newcombe intervals, without multiplicity correction; no population-level curve confidence claim is made. The release’s unknown sampling mechanism limits propensity interpretation and policy transport. Model row predictions and fitted models remain local; only aggregate evaluation tables are published.

Reusable experiment design

Is a proposed experiment ready to run?

Worked example: real control conversion baseline 0.1938%, assumed +20% relative lift, 85:15 allocation, two-sided α = 0.05 and 80% desired power. The planned effect is an explicit design assumption, not fabricated observations or retrospective “observed power.”

Open full-size chart ↗

This design requires approximately 870,047 participants: 739,540 treatment and 130,507 control. At 500k available participants, achieved power is 56.5%; at 1M it is 85.2%.

The reusable Python readiness() accepts baseline, relative or absolute lift, allocation, alpha, desired power and available N. Outputs include required N per arm, absolute/relative MDE, achieved power and readiness. Uses the arcsine two-proportion normal approximation; no clustered-design correction.

Case study A · measurement observability

Can we trust the measurement pipeline?

Daily traffic and measurement definitions are observable. Historical delivery latency and missing source events are not.

Open full-size chart ↗

5 metric/day review flags meet |z| ≥ 3 against the prior seven eligible days. Current observations are excluded from their own baseline. Initial warmup and first/last source days are excluded from alert decisions. Alerts are exploratory and correlated; no multiple-testing correction.

Recommendation: investigate campaign mix, traffic changes and attribution-day alignment for flagged days before declaring broken tracking. Canonical conversion join loss, duplicate replay IDs and attribution-weight errors are all zero in the verified run. Unknown missing-event or arrival-lateness rates remain null.

Days are relative offsets, not invented calendar dates. “Conversions” are 30-day last-click-proxy conversions placed on the selected clicked-impression day; “attributed conversions” are publisher-credited conversions placed on latest linked-impression day. Their daily ratio can reflect differing placement conventions. Original duplicate events cannot be inferred from equal-valued rows; source row IDs permit replay checks only.

Measurement framework

Four complementary questions

01

Attribution

Who gets credit?

02

Incrementality

What happened because of advertising?

03

Uplift modeling

Who responds incrementally to treatment?

04

Monitoring

Can we trust the measurement pipeline?

Use attribution to reconcile credit definitions; randomized assignment to estimate an experiment contrast; uplift to propose a targeting test; and monitoring to assess measurement reliability. Combine these in an advertiser’s own matched measurement program before optimizing for incremental return.

Unavailable by design: actual monetary ROAS / incremental ROAS, same-campaign attribution-versus-causal comparisons, geo effects, MMM and GeoLift. Dataset A costs are transformed and Dataset B has no campaign-level spend or revenue. We do not fabricate these relationships or metrics.

Reproducible evidence

From source files to an auditable report

Checksum-pinned publisher parquet → bounded-memory DuckDB event tables → seven analytical SQL modules → QA → full-release experiment statistics → cached uplift evaluation → aggregate reporting. The existing Python package, event cleaning, cloud adapter and Airflow DAG are extended; Hillstrom remains a supplementary earlier example.

Execution status: local DuckDB + Python analyses executed on real data. BigQuery-compatible pipeline implemented; local DuckDB execution verified. BigQuery service execution and Airflow runtime deployment remain unverified. GitHub Pages serves these static results; it does not run the data pipeline.
